content:
"Instead of getting rid of winter pruning by burning it or feeding it into a shredder, consider turning those cut branches into a dead hedge. This is a practical and attractive way to reuse garden waste, and it can do several jobs at once. A structure like this can help slow strong winds, create useful shelter for birds, insects and other wildlife, and also serve as a natural boundary between different parts of the garden. To make one, drive sturdy stakes or unwanted fence posts into the ground in two parallel lines, leaving roughly 50cm between them. Then stack the pruned material in the gap, starting with the thickest branches near the bottom. As more cuttings are added over time, the hedge will gradually sink and compact.

If the festive season failed to bring you any worthwhile presents, you might lift your spirits by reserving a copy of The Book Of Seeds, published by Ivy Press at £30. Written by Paul Smith, previously the leader of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank, the book is due out in February. It offers a lavishly illustrated exploration of 600 remarkable and striking plant species, featuring everything from dark seeds with amusingly dramatic tufts of hair to orchid seeds so tiny they are barely larger than a speck.

For planting, winter-blooming clematis is especially rewarding. Given a warm, protected and sunny location, it can provide waves of flowers through the coldest part of the year, from December into February. Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ and C. cirrhosa var. balearica both produce cream-coloured, fragrant flowers marked with rich maroon tones, while C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’ bears clear white flowers and can grow even larger. Is there anything else I can help with?"
